scenes.visual: Title card 'Why a Mouse Needs Plumbing' over a flat planarian outline beside a mouse silhouette. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: surface/skin GOLD; oxygen BLUE dots and BLUE gradient; pumped fluid (blood, air, sap) RED; oxygen-starved core DARK GREY; heat ORANGE; mouse and human silhouettes plain charcoal outlines. Symbols on screen: s for a cube's side, L for distance, b for the exponent, M for mass. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Cream background, 16:9. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A flatworm has no lungs and no heart. A mouse has both. What changed when the body got bigger?
scenes.visual: Left: a flat planarian outline glides slowly across the frame, label 'no lungs, no heart'. Right: a mouse silhouette with a small RED heart and pale lungs drawn inside, label 'lungs and heart'. A question mark pulses between them.
scenes.narration: A flatworm has no lungs and no heart. A mouse has both. What changed when the body got bigger?

scenes.tts: Everything a body takes in must cross a surface, oxygen included.
scenes.visual: The mouse outline fades. The planarian's outer edge glows GOLD; small BLUE dots drift in across the GOLD edge from outside.
scenes.narration: Everything a body takes in must cross a surface, oxygen included.

scenes.tts: Take a tiny cube of living tissue. Its gold faces are its surface, and its inside is its volume. Now make every side twice as long.
scenes.visual: A single cube, side labelled 's = 10 um', GOLD faces, rotates slowly. A bracket stretches to 's = 20 um' as a larger cube assembles from eight copies of the small cube, two layers of four.
scenes.narration: Take a tiny cube of living tissue. Its gold faces are its surface, and its inside is its volume. Now make every side twice as long.

scenes.tts: The big cube holds eight times as much inside. But its outer surface grows only four times. So each bit of inside now has half as much surface to feed it.
scenes.visual: Counters tick up beside the big cube: 'volume x 8', 'surface x 4'. Then a ratio readout changes from '0.6 per um' to '0.3 per um', with '6/s' written beneath (computed).
scenes.narration: The big cube holds eight times as much inside. But its outer surface grows only four times. So each bit of inside now has half as much surface to feed it.

scenes.tts: There is a second change, and it matters more. The centre of the big cube now sits twice as far from any face. Oxygen must travel farther.
scenes.visual: A BLUE dot marks the centre of each cube; a dashed line runs from each centre to the nearest GOLD face, labelled '5 um' and '10 um'.
scenes.narration: There is a second change, and it matters more. The centre of the big cube now sits twice as far from any face. Oxygen must travel farther.

scenes.tts: Oxygen gets in by diffusion. Each molecule wanders in random steps, as likely backward as forward.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the small cube. One BLUE dot takes a jittery random walk from the GOLD face inward, leaving a faint trail; a stopwatch in the corner runs. Many dots follow, spreading inward.
scenes.narration: Oxygen gets in by diffusion. Each molecule wanders in random steps, as likely backward as forward.

scenes.tts: Across five micrometres, that walk takes about a hundredth of a second. Now double the distance to ten micrometres. How much longer does the walk take?
scenes.visual: Stopwatch shows '0.0125 s' for 'L = 5 um'. A second track, twice as long, appears beside it with an empty stopwatch and a question card: 'L = 10 um: how long?'
scenes.narration: Across five micrometres, that walk takes about a hundredth of a second. Now double the distance to ten micrometres. How much longer does the walk take?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; a 5-second ring timer counts down at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Four times as long. Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance. Twice as far costs four times the wait, and ten times as far costs a hundred.
scenes.visual: Second stopwatch fills to '0.05 s', label 'x 4'. The formula 't = L² / 2D' writes itself under both tracks (computed, D = 1,000 um² per s).
scenes.narration: Four times as long. Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance. Twice as far costs four times the wait, and ten times as far costs a hundred.

scenes.tts: That is quick across a cell. Now zoom out to one centimetre, about a finger's width. The same random walk takes about fourteen hours.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back far: the cell shrinks to a speck beside a fingertip outline with a bracket '1 cm'. A clock face spins to '≈ 14 hours'.
scenes.narration: That is quick across a cell. Now zoom out to one centimetre, about a finger's width. The same random walk takes about fourteen hours.

scenes.tts: So picture a solid ball of living tissue, breathing only through its gold skin. Oxygen soaks in from the surface, and the tissue burns it on the way in.
scenes.visual: A sphere in cross-section, GOLD rim. A BLUE gradient soaks inward from the rim, fading toward the centre, label 'oxygen used on the way in' (schematic).
scenes.narration: So picture a solid ball of living tissue, breathing only through its gold skin. Oxygen soaks in from the surface, and the tissue burns it on the way in.

scenes.tts: Tissue holds little dissolved oxygen, about a minute's worth or less at resting mammal rates. So supply must keep pace. In this ideal model, a big enough ball runs out at its centre.
scenes.visual: The ball grows steadily, BLUE gradient fading inward. Past a marker, a DARK GREY core opens at the centre, label 'ideal model; core size schematic' (not positioned with any computed depth).
scenes.narration: Tissue holds little dissolved oxygen, about a minute's worth or less at resting mammal rates. So supply must keep pace. In this ideal model, a big enough ball runs out at its centre.

scenes.tts: How big can the ball get before its centre just runs dry? In this model, slow tissue allows a little over a millimetre of radius. Busy tissue allows only a few tenths of a millimetre.
scenes.visual: Two separate balls side by side, no dark core in either; each centre only just fades to zero BLUE. Left ball's radius bracket: 'limiting radius, slow tissue ≈ 1.45 mm'; right, smaller ball: 'limiting radius, busy tissue ≈ 0.19 mm' (computed from an ideal steady-state diffusion model).
scenes.narration: How big can the ball get before its centre just runs dry? In this model, slow tissue allows a little over a millimetre of radius. Busy tissue allows only a few tenths of a millimetre.

scenes.tts: A flatworm takes another route. It grows long and wide, but stays thin. Every cell stays close to the outside, so diffusion is enough.
scenes.visual: The slow-tissue ball morphs into a thin planarian-shaped sheet; BLUE fills it from both faces. Arrows show the sheet stretching mostly in length and width; its thickness bracket grows only a little. No depth number is shown on the sheet.
scenes.narration: A flatworm takes another route. It grows long and wide, but stays thin. Every cell stays close to the outside, so diffusion is enough.

scenes.tts: A mouse is thick, and its tissue runs fast. So it moves fluid in bulk. Pumped air and pumped blood carry oxygen most of the way in.
scenes.visual: A mouse silhouette in cross-section. RED channels branch through it from a beating heart; air flows into branching lungs. BLUE dots ride inside the RED stream deep into the body.
scenes.narration: A mouse is thick, and its tissue runs fast. So it moves fluid in bulk. Pumped air and pumped blood carry oxygen most of the way in.

scenes.tts: Bulk flow brings the supply close, but it does not finish the job. Diffusion still carries oxygen across the last few micrometres, through thin walls.
scenes.visual: Zoom to one RED vessel beside a block of tissue: BLUE dots step out of the RED stream and diffuse a short gap into the cells, label 'last few micrometres: diffusion'.
scenes.narration: Bulk flow brings the supply close, but it does not finish the job. Diffusion still carries oxygen across the last few micrometres, through thin walls.

scenes.tts: So, for the same shape fed only from outside, a bigger body means a longer path. Bodies stay thin, add inner surface, or pump fluid. In thick, busy animals, bulk flow does most of the carrying.
scenes.visual: Split recap: left, the two cubes with 'surface x 4, volume x 8'; right, the stopwatch '2 x distance = 4 x time'; below, three small icons labelled 'stay thin' (flatworm), 'add inner surface' (folded lung) and 'pump fluid' (RED-plumbed mouse); small caption 'same shape, fed from outside'.
scenes.narration: So, for the same shape fed only from outside, a bigger body means a longer path. Bodies stay thin, add inner surface, or pump fluid. In thick, busy animals, bulk flow does most of the carrying.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'Same shape, bigger body, longer path: stay thin, add surface, or pump.'
